title: Field bootstrap recovery heuristics — baremetal & vSphere playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a field-oriented playbook for recovering failed or partially failed Kubernetes bootstraps across two common on-prem surfaces: direct bare-metal (PXE/iPXE -> Ignition) and vSphere-backed ephemeral or persistent node provisioning. Focus is on fast triage, deterministic recovery steps, Terraform module considerations for idempotency, and safe upgrade/rollback heuristics when a bootstrap is stuck or cluster control-plane is degraded.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target: customer-managed clusters created by Redwood Private bootstrap tooling (ignition/ipxe, terraform modules, image builder).
- We assume clusters use an immutable-control-plane approach where control-plane instances are provisioned via Terraform and configured via Ignition/Cloud-init.
- Networking basics (BMC, vCenter, TFTP, DHCP) are reachable from field ops.
- This playbook is for operator/SE use; many steps include quick commands and a longer remediation path.

Quick triage checklist (5–10 min):
1) Confirm failure mode: control-plane not Ready, kubelet flapping, machines stuck in provisioning, or network DHCP/TFTP issues.
2) Collect logs: last 100 lines of kubelet and kube-apiserver, journalctl -u kubelet, systemd-analyze blame on control-plane node.
3) Check provisioning tooling status: terraform apply exit codes, cloud-init/ignition errors in /var/log/cloud-init.log or /var/log/ignition.
4) Verify hardware reachability: ping, ipmitool chassis status, and vCenter VM power state.
5) If unsure, pause automated reconciliation (terraform apply / automation) to avoid fighting manual fixes.

Commands cheat-sheet (use with caution):
- Check node status from admin host (if API is up): kubectl get nodes -o wide
- Describe failing pods: kubectl -n kube-system describe pod <pod>
- Read kubelet journal: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager
- Inspect ignition/cloud-init failures: sudo cat /var/log/ignition | tail -n 200 ; sudo cat /var/log/cloud-init.log
- BMC: ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -P <pass> chassis power status
- vSphere: govc vm.info -json -k "${GOVC_URL}" -u "${GOVC_USER}:${GOVC_PASS}" | jq '.' ; govc vm.power -on <vm>
- TFTP + iPXE: check tftpd log /var/log/daemon.log and tcpdump -i <if> port 69

Scenario-based recovery steps (prioritize shortest impact first):
A) PXE/iPXE never reaches Ignition stage (DHCP/TFTP mismatch)
  1. Verify DHCP lease: dhcpd.leases or check DHCP server for expected MAC->IP mapping.
  2. On TFTP box: tail -f /var/log/daemon.log and confirm file requests for pxelinux.0 or ipxe.efi.
  3. If file missing, upload correct iPXE binary and restart tftpd.
  4. If network ACLs changed, open UDP 67/68 and 69 between provisioning network and host.
  5. As a temporary workaround, provision with a USB image and skip PXE (notes below).

B) Ignition/Cloud-init applied but kubelet fails to register
  1. SSH into the node using BMC console or vCenter console. Check /var/log/ignition and /var/log/cloud-init-output.log.
  2. Validate kubeadm/kubelet config: sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/kubeadm.conf ; sudo cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
  3. Restart kubelet: sudo systemctl restart kubelet && journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager
  4. Check certificate permission issues: ls -l /var/lib/kubelet/pki ; fix owner/group to root:root and restart.
  5. If kubelet is OOM/killed frequently, inspect dmesg and adjust systemd cgroup CPU/memory limits temporarily.

C) Control-plane static pods not coming up (etcd or apiserver crash loops)
  1. Get container logs from kubelet-managed static pods: sudo crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver ; sudo crictl logs <id>
  2. If etcd cannot start due to WAL corruption, follow WAL recovery: move faulty wal directory and restore from snapshot (document location of snapshots in customer installs).
  3. If certificate SAN mismatch after hostname or IP change, regenerate control-plane certs with kubeadm certs renew and rotate. Note: certificate rotation requires all control-plane hosts to be coordinated.

D) vSphere VM provisioned but never joins cluster
  1. Check vCenter task logs from GOVC or vSphere UI (time-of-provision).
  2. Confirm guest customization scripts ran: check cloud-init logs inside VM.
  3. If VM has incorrect network profile (wrong port group), attach to correct port group and power-cycle the VM.
  4. If disk image or template mismatch (old kernel or missing agent), reprovision from updated template.

Terraform module notes (field-friendly reminders):
- Always run terraform plan and save the plan file locally (terraform plan -out plan.tfplan). If you need to undo an automated change, we can reapply the previous plan as a reference.
- Modules should be idempotent: provisioning resources must tolerate machine reboots/power-cycles without creating duplicates. Use lifecycle.ignore_changes for provider-managed metadata fields we do not control in playbook.
- Expose a module var bootstrap_pause (bool) which, when true, will create the VMs but stop before cloud-init/ignition is triggered — useful to hand off to on-site ops to debug network first.
- Store per-cluster bootstrap artifacts (ignition blobs, machine manifests) in a known S3/GCS path with prefix cluster/<cluster-id>/bootstrap/ so we can reapply exact configs.
- When remediating state by hand, keep a copy of the Terraform state before making ephemeral changes; prefer using terraform state mv/replace instead of manual deletion where possible.

Upgrade and rollback heuristics (control-plane and node):
- Upgrade control-plane first in a staggered manner: cordon + drain control-plane replacement (if immutable CP, create new control-plane VM with new version, join, then decommission old).
- Avoid simultaneous etcd upgrades across all control-plane hosts. Ensure etcd health after each step: kubectl get --raw '/healthz/etcd' or etcdctl endpoint health with correct certs.
- In a failed kubelet upgrade (node kernel/module mismatch), revert by reprovisioning the node from previous template image. Keep the old image available for 30 days after upgrade.
- Rollback plan: if majority of control-plane are unhealthy after upgrade, immediately stop automation and follow emergency rollback: recreate previous control-plane VMs from snapshots (if available) and reattach etcd disks. Document exact snapshot ids in terraform outputs at upgrade time.

Observability & telemetry checks to collect early:
- From failing node: journalctl -u kubelet -b --no-pager > /tmp/kubelet.log ; upload to support bundle.
- From provisioning host: tftpd, dhcpd, and dnsmasq logs, plus tcpdump capture of DHCP handshake.
- From control-plane host: /var/log/pods for static pod logs (apiserver, controller-manager, etcd).
- Ensure we capture Terraform state file timestamps and last modification who/when (use git or storage object versioning).

Field hack options (use as last resort):
- Boot a rescue image and manually apply the ignition JSON via machine-config-installer (for RHCOS-like flows).
- Temporarily add an external etcd member and let control-plane reconfigure (complex, document with a runbook).
- Bring up a temporary API proxy that responds with minimal endpoints to allow kubeadm joins to proceed (used in extreme edge cases).

Post-incident notes to record (for each incident):
- Exact commands run, output snippets, and which Terraform plan/state was active.
- If a manual image or template was used as a workaround, record the template checksum and where it’s stored.
- Time-to-recover and which customers (if applicable) were affected.
- Followups: write a small automated test that reproduces the failure mode (e.g., simulate missing TFTP file), add regression guard in CI.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide canonical location for storing per-cluster Ignition blobs (current options: internal S3 vs GCS bucket vs artifact registry).
- Add a terraform variable to expose the ignition SHA to the state output for quick validation in field.
- Build a small CLI that wraps common field commands (govc, ipmitool, tftp checks) and produces a support bundle.

Helpful links & references:
- Internal: CONFLUENCE-PI/Bootstrap-Patterns (linked above)
- Jira: JIRA-RED-8421 — previous incident where vSphere guest customization failed due to template kernel mismatch.
- Scripts: git+ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-scripts.git#pr/212 (field helpers for ipmi/govc).

Notes to self (quick reminders):
- When asking site ops for BMC creds, request temporary cred with expiry and log access.
- If provisioning in a new datacenter, run pre-flight DHCP/TFTP smoke script 24–48 hours prior.
- Keep at least one spare bootable USB image with our minimal rescue OS for bare-metal-only shops.

End of playbook (this is a working draft — expect edits after next field run).
